newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.N.'s Annan, Mandela discuss Zaire, Angolan peace.
newsitem.headline: U.N.'s Annan, Mandela discuss Zaire, Angolan peace.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan said after talks with South African President Nelson Mandela on Thursday the Security Council would consider sending troops to backup a ceasefire in Zaire.
Annan, visiting Africa for the first time as head of the United Nations, said he was optimistic that a summit scheduled in Lome, Togo, on March 26 would lead Zaire towards peace.
He said both sides had accepted a five-point U.N. peace plan in principle and added:
"Both the protaganists have indicated that if they were to sign a ceasefire agreement they would be looking to the U.N. to put in place a monitoring mechanism.
"If a ceasefire is agreed to the (Security) Council will have to consider the possibility of establishing a monitoring mechanism and that can only be done by troops."
Annan said he was optimistic that Wednesday's summit of African leaders and the Lome summit next week would put the country on the road to peace.
"If one can have a ceasefire, if one can have talks and if one can arrange the disengagement of forces and eventually elections, why not go that route?
"Why fight, why kill, why devastate the countryside. That (ceasefire) option is also very much on the table and I hope that's the way we will go," he told reporters.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has seized more than a fifth of Zaire and has vowed to press on until the capital Kinshasa falls.
Rebel commissioner for foreign affairs Kakudji Gaetan told Reuters in Goma on Thursday a ceasefire could only follow after direct talks with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The U.N. is trying to get the two sides to agree to a ceasefire and simultaneous direct negotiations.
"What is important to note is that no one, not even the rebel leaders, have pressed for secession or the breakup of Zaire," Annan said.
"What they say they are seeking is change in leadership. That change in leadership can be attained in many other ways, including through the ballot box," he said.

Mandela, who launched an inconclusive personal initiative earlier this month to bring the two sides together in Cape Town, said he believed rebel leader Laurent Kabila was committed to a negotiated settlement.

"In almost all the discussions we have had with him, he is insisting on meeting President Mobutu. Despite the successes he has achieved in the battlefield, he realises the importance of negotiations," he said.
Mandela said he and Annan also discussed the delayed installation of a government of national unity in Angola, the Sudan, the Middle East tension and plans to restructure the United Nations.
In response to a question, Mandela reiterated his opposition to a U.S. plan floated last year for an African Crisis Response Force trained and financed by the West, but staffed by Africans.

"That initiative should come from Africa, not from outside. I expressed concern about people outside the continent sidelining the leaders on the spot and that situation is one that I find unacceptable," he said.
Annan countered that the United States had refined its position and had taken account of reservations expressed by Mandela and other African leaders.

"The situation has evolved quite considerably since the Americans first put the idea forward and they see it very much as building on African capacity, working with African governments and the U.N. to enhance African capacity.
